body:
So the first problem that I can see with this implementation is that it makes multi-threaded physics behave the same as single-threaded physics. Normally when using multi-threaded physics, ```step()``` is called after ```end_sync()``` so that the step can be performed on another thread at the same as everything else on the main thread until ```_physics_process()``` happens again and the threads are synced. With this addition, the main thread immediately synchronizes with the physics server and does nothing while it waits for the physics step to be completed.

~~I think if you wanted to have a ```_late_physics_process()``` callback, some tradeoffs would have to be made and it would not be exactly the same as ```_physics_process()```. Is it necessary to have access to the physics server during this callback? If not, the physics server does not need to be synced. Updated transforms, area overlaps, etc. are still accessible when not synced with the physics server. In this case I think it would be more appropriate to call it something like ```_post_physics_process()```, as instead of being like ```_physics_process()``` in capabilities, it just happens after.~~
Nevermind, if the physics hasnt stepped then the transforms etc. wont be updated yet. Instead you could take advantage of callbacks such as ```NOTIFICATION_TRANSFORM_CHANGED``` and ```PhysicsServer3D.area_set_monitor_callback()```.

What you might be able to do is instead of putting the callback in the main loop, you could add some callback system to the physics servers so that at the end of the step they run the callbacks on their own threads. It could look something like ```PhysicsServer3D.add_post_step_callback(callable: Callable)``` and ```PhysicsServer3D.remove_post_step_callback(callable: Callable)```. It might also be doable with signals but I don't know if signals / coroutines work across threads.
